questions.prompt: You COPY a secret into an image in one Dockerfile line and `rm` it in the next line. Is the secret still in the image?
choices: No, rm removes it from the image
Yes, it is still in the earlier layer; the later layer only hides it
Only if the image is pushed to a registry
questions.explanation: Each instruction adds a layer. A later layer records a whiteout that hides the file in the merged view, but the bytes stay in the earlier layer and ship with the image.

questions.prompt: What identifies a layer inside an image?
choices: The SHA-256 digest of its content
A random UUID assigned by the daemon
questions.explanation: Layers are content-addressed. Two images built from the same base share the same layer digests, which is why pulls and pushes skip layers that already exist.

questions.prompt: You change one line in your application code. Why does `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` rerun if COPY . . comes before it?
choices: The cache is invalidated top-down: once a layer's input changes, every later instruction is rebuilt
questions.explanation: Build cache is a prefix match on the layer chain. Copy dependency manifests first, install, then copy the rest of the source so code edits do not bust the install layer.

questions.prompt: In the audit tool, what does a `.wh.` entry inside a layer tarball mean?
choices: A file that must be made writable
A whiteout: the path with that name from lower layers is hidden
questions.explanation: OverlayFS-style whiteouts are how a read-only layer stack expresses deletion. `.wh..wh..opq` hides an entire directory from lower layers.

questions.prompt: Which change removes a secret from an image for good?
choices: Adding RUN rm after the COPY
Rebuilding so the secret is never written to a layer (build secrets or a multi-stage build), then re-pushing under a new digest
questions.explanation: Only layers that never contained the secret are safe. Rotate the secret too: anyone who pulled the old digest has it.

questions.prompt: A container writes 2 GB of logs to /var/log inside itself. Where do those bytes live?
choices: In the container's thin writable layer, which is discarded when the container is removed
questions.explanation: Images are read-only. Each container gets a writable layer on top; `docker commit` would freeze it into a new image layer, which is how accidental multi-GB images are born.
